en: The Scripture on the Arising of Deeds, Volume One, also titled the Scripture on the Solemn Admonition of Past Causes and Conditions, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty from the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he dwelt within the Bamboo Grove.
The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus and the arhats with supernormal powers:
"Each of you take the alms-food you have received and together go to the Anavatapta Spring."
The route passed through the kingdom of the five surnames; there, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, he went among them to beg for food.
By means of his supernormal power, he descended from the air, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus.
Arriving at the great Anavatapta Spring, the World-Honored One sat within it.
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, the bhikṣus continued to eat.
At the very time of this meal, the earth shook with a great trembling.
A bhikṣu asked the World-Honored One:
"Why does this earth tremble?
The World-Honored One then explained it for him, out of compassion for these sentient beings who were shaken:
“In hell there are sinners who have committed the most extreme and manifold evils;
a thousand spirits hack their two great ribs,
never resting for even a moment, while their axes and hatchets are all glowing red with fire.”
"Having been hacked for a full thousand years, it was only when my strength was utterly exhausted that I could finally sever [the blade]. He asked:
"What kind of offense did you commit to bring about such agony?"
"This rib is so large; what has caused the earth to tremble?
"This was originally a man of the world who always took pleasure in the wives of others.
Because he sat greedily for sensual desire, he further killed a lay devotee."
"Because of these past conditions, he has attained this great body;
there are a thousand spirits who constantly carve at his two ribs.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One, and the Buddha questioned those of the four paths:
"What conditions have you cultivated?
Each of you should speak for yourselves.
You great disciples of supernormal powers are able to continue turning the Wheel of Dharma."
The wise Śāriputra arose and questioned the World-Honored One:
“O World-Honored One, you are without peer; there is nothing you do not see or hear.
May the World-Honored One first speak for yourself of the various causes and conditions of past lives.”
Sundarī gave rise to malicious slander, hoping thereby to gain his veneration;
yet she slandered the Honored One without cause—what was the karmic condition for this?
Seated at Śrāvastī were these five hundred bhikṣus.
To slander others without cause—what is the karmic condition for this?
Why does one suffer from a headache?
When one executes or kills one's five close relatives, every joint of the body aches.
Furthermore, he suffered from stiffness in his back;
a rigid wooden spear pierced his foot;
and Devadatta hurled a rock from a cliff, which shattered the big toe of his foot.
What is the cause and condition for this?
A garrulous young woman, carrying a basin upon her belly,
has come without cause to slander me here in the midst of the great assembly.
Furthermore, while in the city of Verañjā, he ate horse-grams for three months;
when the brahmin state preceptor invited him, what was the cause and condition for this?
While at Uruvelā, he practiced austerities for a full six years.
"His breath has ceased and he is emaciated from meditation; what is the cause and condition for this?
The World-Honored One explained to him:
"Śāriputra, listen attentively."
Now I shall explain for you in full The conditions of her past lives. **The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes and Conditions of Sundarī** Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was at the Great Anavatapta Pond, together with five hundred great bhikṣus. All were arhats, possessing the six supernatural powers and the power of psychic travel; they were of great renown, handsome and beautiful, each endowed with various marks. They were neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark, neither fat nor thin; their complexions were like red lotuses, and all had brought their minds and senses under control—with the sole exception of one bhikṣu. Who was he?

"It was Ānanda. Then Śāriputra rose from his flowered seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee upon the lotus seat. Facing the Buddha with palms joined, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"The World-Honored One sees nothing that is not seen, hears nothing that is not heard, and knows nothing that is not known. The World-Honored One is without peer; all evils are extinguished and all virtues are universally complete. The devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, subjects, and all sentient beings—all desire to be delivered by him."
World-Honored One, why do you still have remaining karmic conditions?
We pray that the Buddha will himself explain these conditions, so that gods, humans, and all sentient beings who hear them may attain understanding and liberation.
By what causes and conditions did Sundarī come to slander you?
By what causes and conditions was Śyāmāvatī slandered, along with the five hundred arhats?
By what causes and conditions did the World-Honored One suffer a headache?
By what causes and conditions did the World-Honored One suffer pain in his joints?
By what causes and conditions did the World-Honored One suffer from stiffness in his back?
By what causes and conditions was his foot pierced by a sharp wooden splinter?
By what causes and conditions did Devadatta hurl a boulder from a cliff at him?
For what reason did this garrulous woman, carrying a basin amidst the great assembly—both those with outflows and those free from outflows—come forward to slander him, saying:
"Why do you not speak of your own household affairs, but instead speak on behalf of others?"
"I am now approaching my time of delivery and shall need ghee and oil.
For what reason, then, did you eat horse barley with five hundred bhikṣus in the city of Verañjā?
"For what reason did you dwell at Uruvilvā, practicing austerities for six years, claiming that you would thereby attain Buddhahood?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Return once more to your flower seat."
"I shall now explain for you the various causes and conditions from past lives.
Śāriputra then immediately returned to his original seat.

Upon hearing that the Buddha was about to expound the Dharma of causal conditions, the Great Dragon King Anavatapta leaped for joy and, out of great delight, fashioned a seven-jeweled lattice canopy for the Buddha; from within the canopy, sandalwood powder and incense rained down, pervading all the seats.
Countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas all came to the Buddha; with palms joined in reverence, they paid their respects and stood surrounding him.
The Buddha then spoke to Śāriputra:
"In a past life, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a gambler named Viśuddhanetra, who was skilled in song and performance."
At that time, there was a courtesan named Mṛgākṣī (Deer-Eyed), who was exceptionally beautiful and of incomparable purity.
Śuddhākṣa went to her place and said to the woman:
"We should go outside together to a grove of trees; let us seek out a pleasant spot to enjoy ourselves."
The girl replied, "So be it.
Mṛgāra then returned home,
dressed himself in fine garments, and went to the house of Viśākhā.
Viśuddhanetra then prepared a fine carriage and, together with Mṛgāra, set out from the city of Vārāṇasī; they went to a grove of trees where they enjoyed themselves together.
After passing a day and night, Viśuddhanetra beheld her garments and their exquisite beauty, and immediately conceived a covetous mind, thinking:
"I shall kill this woman and take her clothes."
He further thought:
"Once he is killed, how shall I hide him?
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Nirvāṇarata (Delighting in Non-action) not far from where he resided within this garden.
Netra then thought again:
"After this Pratyekabuddha has entered the city for alms in the morning, I shall kill the deer-marked man, bury him within his hut, and return with his robes; who would know my whereabouts?"

At dawn the next morning, the Pratyekabuddha entered the city to beg for food. Following behind him, Netra killed the deer-like man, stripped off his clothes and took them, and buried the corpse within the hut of the one who delights in non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Having leveled the ground as it was before, he then mounted his carriage and entered the city through another gate.
"At that time, the king of Vārāṇasī was named Brahmadaṇḍa.
When the people of the kingdom did not see Mṛgajā, they reported it to the king; the multitude addressed the king, saying:
'We do not see Mṛgajā.'"
The king immediately summoned his ministers and sent them throughout the streets and alleys, searching for him door to door.

Having received these instructions, the ministers searched as commanded; finding no trace of him anywhere, they departed the city once more. There, they saw a flock of birds soaring above the trees, and the people thought:
"We have already searched the entire city without success; there must surely be a reason for this, so we should go there together."
He immediately went to the front of the hut of Nandivardhana and searched for the corpse.
The ministers said to Nandivardhana, "You have already committed an impure act; why did you kill him again?"
The Pratyekabuddha remained silent and did not answer.
When he was questioned in this manner up to three times, he did not answer as before.
Because his hands and feet were pressed into the earth due to the causes and conditions of his previous lives, he remained silent and did not respond.
The ministers then bound Nandivardhana crosswise and interrogated him with beatings.
A tree spirit manifested half of its body and said to the crowd,
"Do not beat this man."
The ministers asked,
"Why did you not strike him?
The spirit replied:
"This man has no such dharma; he will never practice this.
Although the ministers heard the deity’s words, they were unwilling to heed or follow them. Taking this "joyful non-action" as their guide, they went directly to the king's presence and said to him:
"This ascetic, having committed an impure act, has furthermore killed [the deity]."
Upon hearing these words, the king cried out in great wrath and said to his ministers:
"Look at this ascetic! Is it proper for him to act in such an unrighteous manner?"
The King commanded his ministers:

"Quickly bind him to a donkey and beat the drums as you parade him through the city. Then, exit through the southern gate and lead him beneath a tree; impale him upon an iron spear fixed atop a pole, and have archers shoot at him with bows.
If he does not die, then cut off his head."
The ministers, having received their instructions, quickly bound the donkey and loaded it, beating drums as they paraded through the streets.
When the people of the country saw this, they all wondered at the reason; some believed it, while others did not. A great crowd gathered to watch, wailing and lamenting in sorrow.

At that time, Viśuddhanetra was hiding within a broken wall. Hearing the clamor of the multitude, he leaned out from the wall and peered through it; seeing the Muni bound in reverse fetters and led away by a donkey, while the crowd pursued him, he thought to himself:
"This ascetic has been falsely accused for no reason and is about to die; he could not possibly be possessed of lustful desire."
"I killed the deer marked with signs; it was not the Daoist who killed it. I shall receive death myself so that the Daoist may live.
Having thought this, Jingyan ran out toward the great assembly and cried out to the officials:
"Do not torment and kill this Daoist! It was not the Daoist who killed the deer marked with signs; it was I who did so."
"I pray that you release this Daoist and bind me instead; let me be punished according to my crime.
All the high officials were astonished and said, "How can one take another's punishment upon oneself?"
They immediately untied the pratyekabuddha’s bonds together, then seized Net-Eye and bound him as before.
All the high officials and others prostrated themselves before the pratyekabuddha and repented, saying:

"We were foolish and, without cause, unjustly tormented you, O Master. We pray that through your great compassion, you will pardon our offenses and not cause us to suffer such heavy calamity in the future."
Thus he spoke three times, but the Pratyekabuddha, who delights in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), remained silent and did not answer.
The Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"It is not fitting for me to enter the city of Vārāṇasī again to beg for alms; I shall instead attain parinirvāṇa right here before this assembly."

The Pratyekabuddha then leaped up into the air before the assembly, moving back and forth therein, sitting, reclining, standing, and walking; from his waist downward he emitted smoke, while from his waist upward he emitted fire;
or again, from his waist downward he emitted fire, while from his waist upward he emitted smoke;
or from his left flank he emitted smoke, while from his right flank he emitted fire.
Sometimes fire issued from his left side and smoke from his right side;
sometimes smoke issued from his front and fire from his back;
or sometimes fire issued from his front and smoke from his back.
Sometimes fire issued from below the waist and water from above the waist;
sometimes water issued from below the waist and fire from above the waist;
or fire issued from the left flank and water from the right flank.
In some cases, water issues from the left side of the body and fire from the right;
in others, water issues from the front of the abdomen and fire from the back;
or fire issues from the front of the abdomen and water from the back.
Sometimes water issued from his left shoulder and fire from his right;
sometimes fire issued from his left shoulder and water from his right;
or both shoulders issued water, or both shoulders issued fire.
Thereupon, his entire body emitted smoke, his entire body emitted fire, and his entire body emitted water; then, in mid-air, he incinerated his body and entered parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, the great assembly all wept with grief; some repented, while others prostrated themselves. They took his relics and erected a stūpa at a crossroads.
The officials immediately took Net-Eyed to King Brahmadatta and said, "This man killed the deer; it was not the ascetic who killed it.
The king then grew angry with these supervisors:
"Previously, why did you falsely report a baseless matter, claiming that this man had committed murder, and now say it is not so?
You have caused me to be regarded as a liar and unjustly distressed a Daoist practitioner."
The ministers said to the king:
"At that time, we repeatedly questioned the ascetic, asking why he had killed a man.
The ascetic remained silent and did not answer; furthermore, his hands and feet became stuck to the ground. For these reasons, we concluded that he had committed the murder."
The king then commanded his ministers:
"Load this man upon a donkey and take him to the south of the city. First impale him with a spear, then fix a pole through his head and have a crowd shoot him with bows;
if he does not die, then cut off his head."

The ministers, having received these instructions, immediately loaded him onto a donkey, beat the drums, and paraded him through the entire city. Having done so, they went out south of the city to the foot of a tree, impaled him on a wooden stake with a spear, shot arrows at him from a cluster of bows, and finally decapitated him.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who that Pure-Eyed One was at that time?
It was none other than myself."
Śāriputra! Do you also know the one named Mṛgajā?
She is none other than the present Sundarī.
Śāriputra! Do you know who that King Brahmadatta was at that time?
He is none other than this present-day Śākya, Daṇḍapāṇi.
Śāriputra! At that time, I killed a deer and wrongfully tormented a pratyekabuddha; because of this sin, for countless thousands of years I was boiled in the hells and impaled upon sword-trees;
for countless thousands of years I remained among the animals.
For countless thousands of years, he remained among the hungry ghosts.
Due to the remaining karmic retribution from that time, although he has now become a Buddha, he still suffered this slander from Sundarī.
Thereupon, the Buddha himself spoke these verses on the causes and conditions of his past lives:
“Formerly my name was Viśuddhacakṣus, and I was a gambler.
A Pratyekabuddha named Nandika suffered great hardship because of no fault of his own.
Here is one of true and pure conduct, who is being harassed and distressed by the multitude.”
Having humiliated and bound him, they further sought to drive him out of the city.
Seeing this Pratyekabuddha, distressed and fettered,
I gave rise to a heart of compassion and caused him to attain liberation.
Because of these causes and conditions, I have long endured the sufferings of hell.
Even now, the remnants of that calamity cause me to be slandered.
I shall now sever future births; thus, my existence shall end with this very life.
Because of this Sundarī, he suffered slander;
though the causal conditions may never be escaped, they likewise do not cling to empty space.
One should guard against these three causal conditions, which must never be transgressed from beginning to end.
"I have attained Buddhahood by myself and become the General of the Three Realms;
therefore, I have explained these prior causes and conditions at the Great Anavatapta Spring.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Behold the Tathāgata: all evils have been exhausted and all virtues are universally complete; he is able to deliver devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and subjects, as well as all crawling and wriggling creatures, enabling them all to attain liberation and the peace of nirvāṇa."

Even with such merit, one still cannot escape the influence of past conditions; how much more so for those who are ignorant and have not yet attained the Way, who do not restrain their body, speech, and mind—what shall become of these?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should train in this, as should all arhats and all sentient beings: you must guard the three [precepts] of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind."
“Śāriputra! You should train in this, as well as all others.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, Śāriputra, along with the five hundred arhats, the great nāga king Anavatapta, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha taught, received it with joy and put it into practice.
2. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes and Conditions of Śyāmāvatī. The second [sūtra], "The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes and Conditions of Śyāmāvatī," was thus heard:

At one time, the Buddha was at the Great Pond of Anavatapta, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats possessing the six supernormal powers and spiritual faculties, with the sole exception of one bhikṣu—Ānanda.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a king named Suvyākhyāta, and there was a city called Suvyākhyātakṛta."

There was a brahmin named Yanrudha, who was fond of learning and possessed vast knowledge. He was proficient in the external sciences, the three Vedas, astronomy, diagrams and prophecies, divination and physiognomy, and the arts; he was well-versed in the seven types of scripts as well as the teachings of non-Buddhist schools. Understanding all doctrines and worldly classics, he possessed thirty marks of excellence and constantly taught five hundred youths from noble families.

There was also a brahmin named Brahmā who was immensely wealthy and possessed of great riches, including elephants, horses, the seven treasures, attendants, and servants. His wife’s name was Pure Sound; she was upright and exquisite, of peerless beauty, and her character was harmonious and gentle, free from any sense of jealousy.
Yen Rudaya took Brahmā as his *dānapati* (patron), and his wife, Viśadaghoṣā, provided for Yen Rudaya with food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for illness.
There was a Pratyekabuddha named Priyadarśana who entered the city, carrying his robes and bowl, intending to beg for alms.

He happened upon the gate of Brahmā’s Palace; at that time, Viśvabhū saw the Pratyekabuddha, whose robes were neatly arranged, whose gait was composed and deliberate, and whose six sense-faculties were tranquil and settled. His heart was filled with great affection and joy, and he immediately invited him to receive offerings, saying:
"From this day forward, please accept from me your clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine. For my sake, please accept my invitation."
Śuddhasvara immediately filled his bowl with rich and delicious food and gave it to him.
Having accepted it, the Pratyekabuddha held the bowl and ascended into the air; after circling seven times, he flew back to his dwelling place.
At that time, the people within the city, seeing this supernatural power, said:
"It is our good fortune that such a person exists in our land.
The entire nation rejoiced, making offerings to him without weariness.
“Jingyin’s offerings to the pratyekabuddha increased day by day,
whereas those of Daiyan Ruda gradually diminished.
Once Ruda realized his own offerings had become meager while those of the other had grown substantial, he gave rise to envy and jealousy, speaking words of slander:”
"This Daoist truly possesses no virtue of the precepts. Why is this?
Because he has committed impure acts with this Pure Sound."
"For this reason, we provide him with abundant offerings.
Yan Rudaya then said to his five hundred disciples:
"This practitioner has violated the precepts and lacks diligent application."
The youths each returned to their homes and issued a proclamation, saying:
"This Daoist has no pure conduct; he has had an affair with Jingyin. The youths said:
"Very well! As the Master has said, this practitioner truly possesses a mind of lust.
The five hundred youths, having received these instructions, entered the city and went through the streets, proclaiming:
"This Daoist has a lustful heart; he has had illicit relations with Jingyin.
The people of the country all harbored doubts:
"If his supernormal powers are such as this, could he truly have such a defiled reputation?"
This sound continued for seven years before it ceased.

Subsequently, a Pratyekabuddha manifested the eighteen transformations and entered parinirvāṇa; only then did the multitude realize that Yan Rudaya was a deceiver and that the Pratyekabuddha was pure and holy.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who Yaṇrudā was at that time?
It was none other than myself."
The Brahmā of that time was King Udayana;
the Pure Voice of that time was Śamīvatī;
and the five hundred youths of that time are now these five hundred arhats.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“At that time, because I had lost my offerings, I gave rise to a mind of envy and jealousy, and together with you all, I slandered the pratyekabuddhas. Due to these causes and conditions, I entered hell together with you all, where I was boiled in cauldrons of boiling water for countless thousands of years.”
"Due to these remaining karmic consequences, although I have now attained Buddhahood, I am still subject to the slander of Śamīvat along with you all.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses on the causes and conditions of a previous life:
"In a former life I was a brahmin, Extensively studying the four external schools."
While dwelling in a grove of trees, he instructed five hundred youths.
There was a Pratyekabuddha, pure and endowed with supernatural powers;
seeing that [the teacher] had received offerings, he slandered him groundlessly and without cause.
He returned and told the youths, "The Daoist’s conduct was impure.
When I had just said this, the youths were all filled with joy.
Having heard this, the youths went throughout every street and lane.
They all spoke to the multitude, saying: "The Daoist has committed an impurity.
Because of these causes and conditions, he shall pass through the hells for a long time;
both I and you all shall likewise endure further boundless suffering.
Due to these remaining causes and conditions, this assembly of five hundred people was slandered without cause;
they sat [in meditation] at Śrāvastī. Now that I have attained the Unsurpassed Way in this final age, [I have brought them to liberation].
To slander another without cause— For this, one sits in the śamī tree.
The Tathāgata, having become a Honored Buddha, The Great General of the Three Worlds,
Within the great pool of Anavatapta, Spoke of his own past-life conditions.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Observe the Tathāgata:
all outflows are exhausted and all virtues are universally perfected; out of compassion for devas and humans, even down to crawling insects, he desires to deliver them all.”
"Even though one possesses such merit, one still cannot avoid the influence of past conditions; how much less so for those who are ignorant and have not yet recognized the Way?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should study this, as well as all the Arhats and all sentient beings; everyone should study this."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, you should guard the three [precepts] of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind;
Śāriputra, you should train yourself in this way.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Śāriputra, the five hundred arhats, the great nāga king Anavatapta, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
3. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes of Headache. The third [sūtra], "The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes of Headache," was thus heard:

At one time, the Buddha was at the Great Anavatapta Spring together with five hundred great bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), with the sole exception of one bhikṣu—Ānanda.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In the distant past, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a time of famine when grain was precious. People all abandoned their bodies until only white bones remained; they would beat them, boil them, and drink the broth, or dig up the roots of a hundred kinds of plants to sustain their meager lives."
With one *sheng* of gold, one could purchase one *sheng* of grain.
At that time, there was a large village in Rājagṛha consisting of several hundred households, named Kiu-yue (Kauśāmbī).
Not far to the east of the village was a pond named Many Fishes.
The people of Gijjhakūṭa village took their wives and children to the Many Fishes Pond, stayed by its shore, and caught fish to eat.
At that time, some fishermen had caught fish and placed them on the shore;
as they leaped upon the land, I was then a young child, exactly four years of age, and I rejoiced at seeing the fish leap.
At that time, there were two kinds of fish in the pond:
one was named *piṅgala* and the other was named *bahujihva*.
They spoke to one another, saying:
"We have committed no offense against these people, yet we have been unjustly seen as their food.
In a future life, we must surely take our revenge upon them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you recognize those men and women, great and small, from the village of Kapilavastu at that time?
They are none other than the Śākyas of the kingdom of Kapilavastu today;
the infant of that time was my very self."
At that time, the fish with the parched scales was King Virūḍhaka;
at that time, the garrulous fish was the one who is now the Brahmin soothsayer of King Virūḍhaka, named Duṣjihva (Evil Tongue).
At that time, as the fish leaped, I struck its head with a small staff; by reason of this karma, I fell into hell for countless thousands of years.
Although I have now attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, due to this residual karmic connection, when King Virūḍhaka attacked the Śākyas, I suffered from a headache.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know how it is that I have a headache? Śāriputra!"
When I first experienced a headache, I said to Ānanda:
"Bring a bowl with a capacity of four *śu* filled to the brim with cold water.
Ānanda brought it as instructed; I wiped my forehead with my finger and dropped a drop of sweat into the water, and the water immediately evaporated.
It is like throwing a single drop of water into a great cauldron that has been boiling empty all day; the water is instantly scorched and consumed.
The heat of my headache is of such a nature.
Even if there were overhanging cliffs extending one *yojana* or even a hundred *yojanas* from the side of Mount Sumeru, they too would be utterly consumed by the heat of my headache.
“Śāriputra, such was the headache of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses on past causes:
"In a previous life, in the village of Kukkuta, there was a son of a Kukkuta who caught fish,
placed them on the shore, and struck their heads with a staff.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has passed through the hells for a long time."
It is called the Black Rope Hell, where one is burned and boiled for an exceedingly long time.
Due to these remaining causes and conditions, I now suffer from a feverish headache.
When I killed those Śākyas, I was the evil-doer Vairocana.
This causal condition never transforms, nor does it adhere to empty space.
We should together be self-restrained and guard our body, speech, and mind.
May I myself become a Honored Buddha and attain the status of General of the Three Realms.
"Therefore, I have spoken of the conditions from a previous life at the Great Anavatapta Spring.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"If even the Tathāgata—whose manifold evils are exhausted and all virtues fully perfected—desires that devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, and subjects shall all remember his goodness, yet still requires such conditions, how much more so for those who are ignorant and have not yet attained the Way?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should train in this; all arhats and all sentient beings should likewise train in this.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, you should protect the three [precepts] of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind;
Śāriputra, you should train in this.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Śāriputra, along with the five hundred arhats, the great nāga king Anavatapta, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it.
4. The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Aching Joints Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was at the Great Anavatapta Pond, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. All were arhats endowed with the six supernormal powers, with the sole exception of one bhikṣu—Ānanda.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In the distant past, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was the son of an elder who contracted a fever and became extremely ill."
In that city there was the son of a great physician who was uniquely skilled in identifying various medicines and capable of curing all manner of ailments.
The elder’s son called to this physician’s son and said,
"Cure my illness for me, and I shall give you a great amount of wealth and treasures."
The physician’s son immediately treated him, and the elder’s son recovered from his illness;
yet after his recovery, he did not acknowledge the physician’s service.
Later, when the elder’s son fell ill again, he again ordered him to treat him, and upon recovery, he did not repay his labor.
This was repeated three times, yet he did not reward him as before.
Later, the physician fell ill again and summoned him to treat him;
the physician’s son thought to himself, "Previously, he recovered three times and yet gave me no reward."
The elder’s son said, "You have treated me on previous occasions, but I have not yet repaid you; now that you treat me well, when I am recovered, I shall repay you all at once.
The physician’s son thought to himself:
"Having been deceived in this manner up to three times, like a child being hoodwinked, I shall now punish him so that his life shall be cut short.
He then administered the wrong medicine; the illness consequently grew more severe, and he met his end.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who that physician’s son was at that time?
It was none other than myself."
"The sick son of the elder at that time was Devadatta.

The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "At that time, I gave this son of the elder what was not medicine, which caused him to meet his end. By reason of this, he suffered the torments of burning and boiling in hell, as well as among animals and hungry ghosts, for many thousands of years."
"Because of these remaining karmic conditions, although I have now attained Buddhahood, there still arises this illness of pain and aching in my joints.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses on his past causes and conditions:
"In the past, I was the son of a physician, Treating the child of an elder."
Hatred is not a medicine; because of it, one encounters impermanence.
Due to these past causes and conditions, one has long endured the sufferings of hell;
now, because of remaining causes and conditions, one suffers from afflictions and pain.
Causes and conditions never perish, nor do they cling to empty space.
By means of these three causes and conditions, one fully guards body, speech, and mind.
"I have attained Buddhahood by myself and become the General of the Three Realms;
therefore, I have recounted the conditions of my previous lives at the Great Anavatapta Spring.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"You see that the Tathāgata has exhausted all evils and is universally endowed with all virtues; yet even when he wishes for devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, kings, and subjects to all contemplate his goodness, such conditions still exist—how much more so for those who are ignorant and have not yet attained the Way?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should train in this; the five hundred arhats and all sentient beings should likewise train in this.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, you should protect the three [precepts] of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind;
Śāriputra, you should train in this.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Śāriputra, along with the five hundred arhats, the great nāga king Anavatapta, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Past Causes of Back Pain Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was at the Great Anavatapta Pond, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats possessing the six supernormal powers and spiritual faculties, with the single exception of one bhikṣu—Ānanda.
Thereupon, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In the distant past, during a time of great festival gathering in Rājagṛha, there were two clans of Mallas in that country:
one of the Kṣatriya caste and one of the Brāhmaṇa caste, both of whom also came to the assembly."
At that time, two wrestlers were engaged in a match. The Brahmin wrestler said to the Kṣatriya wrestler, "Do not strike me;
I shall give you a great amount of money and treasures."
The Kṣatriya, therefore, did not exert his full strength, playing a trick to make him submit.
Both men were thus given the title and both received the king’s reward; yet the Brahmin wrestler ultimately did not repay the Kṣatriya wrestler for what he had promised.

When the next festival arrived and they gathered again for the wrestling match, the Brahmin wrestler again sought out the Kṣatriya wrestler. As before, they made an agreement; however, the Kṣatriya wrestler again spared him from fighting and received the aforementioned reward, yet he did not inform the other.
Thus it was repeated three times.
Later, when they met again, the Brahmin Malla spoke once more to the Kṣatriya Malla, saying:
"What you have previously promised, you should now fulfill all at once."
The Kṣatriya strongman thought to himself: "This man has repeatedly deceived me;
since he neither repays my kindness nor refrains from encroaching upon my share, I shall cause him to perish this very day."
The Kṣatriya then gave a dry laugh and said, "You have deceived me three times; from now on, I will no longer use your things.

He then pressed down on the man's neck with his right hand and seized the waist of his trousers with his left, squeezing him between both hands and breaking his spine like a snapped stalk of sugarcane. He lifted him up, spun him around three times so that the crowd could see, and then dashed him to the ground; as soon as he hit the earth, he died.
The king and his ministers were all greatly delighted and bestowed upon him one hundred thousand gold coins.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who it was that, at that time, the Kṣatriya wrestler slew the Brāhmaṇa wrestler?"
"I was that person; the Brahmin wrestler was Devadatta.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"At that time, because of my greed and anger, I struck and killed this wrestler; by reason of these causes and conditions, I fell into hell, where I was burned, boiled, and flogged for several thousand years."
"Now that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, it is due to the remaining conditions of that time that I now suffer from this affliction of back pain.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses regarding his past conditions:
"At a festival, we wrestled together; I intended to defeat that man."
With a single toss, he was thrown to the ground, causing his spine to snap in two.
Because of these causes and conditions, he suffered the pains of hell for a long time;
due to the lingering karmic retribution from his previous life, he now suffers from this ailment of a broken back.
This condition never ceases, nor does it cling to empty space.
Guard these three causal conditions; do not transgress in body, speech, or mind.
"I have become a self-enlightened Buddha, Attaining the rank of General of the Three Realms;
Amidst the Great Spring of Anavatapta, I shall myself recount the karmic conditions of my past lives.
The Buddha spoke thus to Śāriputra:

"You see that although the Tathāgata has exhausted all evils and is universally endowed with all virtues, and though he desires to enable all beings—including devas, nāgas, spirits, emperors, kings, ministers, subjects, and all sentient beings—to cross over [to liberation], he cannot even avoid the remaining karmic retribution; how much less so for those who are ignorant and have not yet attained the Way?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, “You all should train in this:
guard the three [actions] of the body, the four of the mouth, and the three of the mind.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Śāriputra, the five hundred arhats, and the eight classes of spirits and deities, having heard what the Buddha taught, received it with joy and put it into practice.
6. The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Being Pierced by a Wooden Spear Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove Monastery, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At dawn, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus and Ānanda, entered the city of Rājagṛha together with them to beg for food, visiting every household.
He saw within this village a piece of split hard wood, a single plank twelve inches long, which had been cast to one side and stood upright before the Buddha.
The Buddha then thought to himself:
"This is the result of past karma; what I have done myself, I must receive myself.
When the multitude heard and saw this, they all gathered together to watch; upon seeing it, the great assembly was struck with such astonishment that they cried out in alarm.
The Buddha again thought to himself:
"I shall now manifest the retribution for past karmic conditions so that all people may see it, believe in and understand the law of calamity and retribution, and dare not commit evil.
The Buddha then leaped into the air to a height of one *zhang* above the ground; the wooden spear pursued the Buddha, also rising to a height of one *zhang*, and came to a halt before him.
The Buddha ascended further to the height of two-edged, three-edged, four-edged, and even seven-edged spears, and the spear likewise rose to the height of those seven edges;
the World-Honored One ascended another *tāla* tree’s height, and the spear likewise rose to the height of one *tāla*;
the Buddha ascended further until he reached the height of seven *tāla* trees, and the spear followed him upward, standing before the Buddha.
The Buddha ascended another seven *li*, and the spear likewise rose seven *li*;
the Buddha ascended another ten *li*, and the spear did the same;
the Buddha ascended another one *yojana*, and the spear followed him accordingly.
The Buddha ascended further by seven *yojanas*, and the spear likewise rose after him.

In mid-air, the Buddha manifested a blue stone, six *yojanas* thick and twelve *yojanas* in length and breadth; standing upon it, the spear pierced through the stone and emerged, standing before the Buddha.

Again, in mid-air, the Buddha manifested water, twelve *yojanas* in length and breadth and six *yojanas* deep; standing upon the water, the spear again passed over the water and stood before the Buddha.

The Buddha again manifested in the air a great fire, twelve yojanas in length and breadth and six yojanas in height; he stood upon the flames, and the spear likewise passed over the flames and came to stand before the Buddha.

The Buddha again manifested in the air a whirlwind, twelve yojanas in length and breadth and six yojanas in height; he stood upon the wind, and the spear approached from the side at an angle and came to stand before the Buddha.
The Buddha ascended again and stayed within the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings; the spear also came up and stood before the Buddha.
The Buddha ascended again to the Heaven of the Thirty-three; upon a lapis lazuli wall there, one *yojana* in extent, the Buddha stood, and the spear also came up and stood before the Buddha.
After the Buddha had departed, the Four Heavenly Kings said to one another:
"The Buddha fears this wooden spear, yet the spear pursues him without ceasing.
They all agreed in their displeasure and vanished from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by means of transformation.
Upon reaching the Yāma Heaven, the Yāma devas vanished;
upon reaching Tuṣita, the Tuṣita devas vanished;
upon reaching Nirmāṇarati, the Nirmāṇarati devas vanished.
When he reached Varuṇī-madhu, Varuṇī-madhu vanished;
he proceeded to the Brahmā heaven.
The wooden spear ascended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, following in succession upward until it reached the Brahmā heaven, where it stood before the Buddha.
The devas all said to one another,
"The Buddha fears this spear and has fled, yet the spear pursues him without ceasing.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded to the Brahmā devas the Dharma concerning his own past karmic conditions.
Returning from the Brahma Heaven, he went to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he descended to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
from the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, he descended to the Tuṣita Heaven.
From Tuṣita, it extends downward to the Yāma Heaven;
from the Yāma Heaven, downward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, downward to the Cāturmahārājika Heaven.
The Four Heavenly Kings descended back to Rājagṛha;

to all the devas they encountered along the way, they preached the Dharma of past causes and conditions. The spear likewise descended from above to Rājagṛha, and the Buddha also preached the Dharma of past causes and conditions to the people of Rājagṛha.

The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, departed from the city of Rājagṛha; the spear also followed behind the Buddha, and the people of the country all pursued the Buddha out of the city.
The Buddha asked the multitude:
"Where do you intend to go?"
The multitude replied,
"We wish to follow the Tathāgata to observe this causal connection.
The Buddha said to the multitude:
"Each of you should return; the Tathāgata himself knows the proper time.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "Tathāgata!"
"Why did you send the multitude back?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"If the multitude had seen me settle this karmic debt, they would all have died on the spot."
Ānanda remained silent.
The World-Honored One then returned to the Veṇuvana Monastery, entered his own quarters, and instructed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you return to your own rooms."
Each having received the instruction, they returned to their rooms.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What should I do?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"You too should return to your room.
Ānanda immediately returned.
The Buddha then thought to himself:
"This is due to what I myself created in past lives; I must certainly repay it.
He immediately took his great robe, folded it into four layers, and returned to sit upon his original seat.

The Buddha then extended his right foot, and the wooden spear immediately entered downward from the sole of his foot, passing through and penetrating the earth to a depth of sixty-eight thousand yojanas;
it passed this earth and reached the water, the depth of which was also sixty-eight thousand yojanas;
it passed the water and reached the fire, the height of which was sixty-eight thousand yojanas.
When it reached the fire, it was scorched.
At that moment, the earth shook in six ways.
Ānanda and the bhikṣus each thought to themselves:
"Now that the earth has shaken, the spear must have pierced the Buddha's foot.
Once the Buddha was pierced, he experienced bitter pain, sharp pain, agonizing pain, and the pain of suffocating breath.
Ānanda immediately went to where the Buddha was and, seeing the wound from the spear piercing the Buddha’s foot, fainted and fell to the ground.
The Buddha then sprinkled water on Ānanda, and he rose.
Having risen, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rubbed and wiped them, and kissed them; shedding tears and weeping, he said:
“With these feet, the Buddha traveled to the foot of the tree to subdue Māra, and ascended as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother.”
“World-Honored One, how could your Vajra-body have been harmed to such an extent by this small piece of wood?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Cease, do not grieve or weep.”
“Due to the causes and conditions of the world, one revolves through birth and death; such are the sufferings and afflictions.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, “At this moment, how is the pain of your wound—has it increased or decreased?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Gradually there will be those who submit.
Śāriputra, leading the community of bhikṣus, came to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and performed his salutations, he stood to one side.
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
"I wonder how the pain of the wound is— has it increased or decreased?
The Buddha replied to Śāriputra:
"The pain of the ulcer gradually subsides.
At that time, among the assembly of bhikṣus, those whose outflows were not yet exhausted saw this ulcer and all cried out in grief and wept, saying:
"The World-Honored One is of great compassion; there is nothing he does not save. How can it be that there is such a cause for this pain?"
The Buddha said to these bhikṣus: "Cease, do not weep.
I myself created this condition in a previous life; I must inevitably undergo its results, for there is no place from which to escape."

This retribution was not created by the father, nor by the mother, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor was it created by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; it was originally fashioned by myself, and now I myself must experience its consequences.
Those who had attained the superknowledge of the exhaustion of outflows each remained silent and reflected upon a verse formerly spoken by the Buddha:
"Whatever deeds a person performs, Whether they be good or evil acts, These actions return to the self; In the end, they do not perish."
When Jīvaka heard that the Buddha had been pierced by a wooden stake, he wept and went to the place where King Ajātaśatru was.
King Ajātaśatru said, "Why are you weeping?"
Jīva replied, "I heard that the Buddha’s foot had been pierced by a wooden stake; for this reason, I wept.
Upon hearing these words, King Ajātaśatru rose from his bed, fell to the ground in a faint, and remained there for a long while before regaining consciousness.
The entire palace, both inside and out, was filled with alarm and terror.
The King rose and wept, commanding his ministers:
"Quickly prepare the carriage; I wish to go to where the Buddha is."
The ministers received their instructions and immediately prepared the carriage, reporting to the king:
"The carriage is ready. The king then ascended the carriage and departed from the city of Rājagṛha.

When the four castes and clans within the city, as well as the laymen and laywomen of pure faith, heard that the Buddha had been pierced by a wooden stake, the king and his younger brother Jīvaka, along with this multitude of people, surrounded him by hundreds of thousands and together proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
He alighted from his carriage, removed his crown, unfastened his sword, and set aside his parasol, then proceeded on foot to approach the Buddha.

The Buddha was lying on his right side; having paid homage to the Buddha, the king grasped the Buddha’s feet with his hands, rubbed and stroked them, and pressed them to his mouth, identifying himself by the name of his kingdom and his own name:
"I am Ajātaśatru, King of Magadha. I inquire after the World-Honored One: has the pain of your wound diminished even slightly?"
The Buddha replied to Ajātaśatru:
"May the Great King always enjoy peace and security, long life, and freedom from illness.
You should govern by means of the True Dharma and never practice what is contrary to the Dharma."
The Buddha then bade the king take a seat, and the king immediately sat down.
The king asked the Buddha:
"I have heard from the Tathāgata that the Buddha’s body is adamantine and indestructible."
"I do not understand why you have now been pierced by this wooden spear.
The Buddha told the king,
"All phenomena are destroyed by their respective conditions and opposites."
"Although my body is adamantine and cannot be destroyed by a wooden spear, it is destroyed by the force of past karmic retribution.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"What people of the world do, Each sees for themselves through their own actions."
"By performing good deeds one obtains a good retribution; by performing evil deeds one obtains an evil retribution.
Therefore, Great King, you should learn to abandon evil and follow what is good."
The foolish who do not study and have not yet recognized the true Way commit sins with levity and laughter, only to receive their retribution with wailing and weeping later.
For this reason, Great King!
"One should not commit an offense in jest; Your Majesty, you ought to train yourself thus.
The King said to Jīvaka:
"Prepare an excellent medicine, wash the wound, and treat it with mantras, ensuring that he recovers in due time."
Jīva replied, “Yes. Jīva then immediately prostrated before the Buddha,
washed his feet, applied the medicine for healing flesh wounds, and further recited the incantation for relieving pain.
Jīvaka took out a cotton cloth worth hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold, wrapped it around the Buddha’s feet, rubbed them with his hands, and kissed them, saying:
"May the Buddha live long; may this ailment be quickly removed."
"All sentient beings shall also attain liberation from the sufferings of the long night.
He immediately rose, prostrated before the Buddha, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, for the sake of King Ajātaśatru and the entire assembly, the Buddha expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
"What are the Four Noble Truths?

They are the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; these are the Four Noble Truths.
When this was said, sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and achieved liberation of mind.
Eleven thousand people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the king took his leave, saying:
"I have many affairs of state; I wish to return and bid you farewell."
The Buddha said, "It may be so;
you should know that now is the time.
The king immediately rose, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned home.
The various assemblies also each paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and returned.

Then, at evening, at midnight, seven celestial beings arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling; each was capable of producing a hundred kinds of musical sounds. They prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated his seat once, and stood to one side.
One day he said to the Buddha: "Śramaṇa Gautama!
It is like a lion that, having received a wound, can endure the pain without telling anyone."
One day he said again: "Śramaṇa Gautama!
You are like an elephant that, when afflicted by a wound, can endure the pain without speaking of it to others."
One day he spoke again, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! Just as a gayal ox bellows while experiencing pain, yet remains unaware of it."
One day he spoke again, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!
Even when a water buffalo bellows, he does not feel any pain."
One day he spoke again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! You are like the Eight-Armed Heavenly King who, when afflicted with sores, is able to endure the pain."
One day he spoke again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! You are like a noble horse that feels no pain."
One day he spoke again, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama is truly discerning and pure; he does not feel pain."
The first deity said: “O Buddha!

You are the lion among men, the elephant among men, the gayal among men, the buffalo among men, the eight-armed celestial king among men, the precious horse among men, and the one who is discerning and pure among men. World-Honored One, those such as you are able to endure such painful suffering.”
This group of fools endures suffering; the World-Honored One endures it with wisdom.

They are not like the heterodox practitioners and brahmins who, having already passed middle age, become indolent and take wives; thus they hope to transcend suffering, yet have no means by which to attain transcendence.
Why is this? Because it cannot reach ultimate completion.

Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is pure completion; all cravings and desires are severed, and through the extinction of all things, one attains Nirvāṇa. It is only in this way that one crosses over the foul ocean of the triple world.
"Why is this? Because these individuals possess right concentration of mind, seeking nirvana through the Four Noble Truths.
Thereupon, the deva spoke in verse:
"Vicious and wild, difficult to subdue; Deluded and doubtful, lacking settled wisdom.
With a distracted will, dwelling in the wilderness like the dews, One does not cross over the abyss of birth and death.
Settled wisdom eliminates the wicked and the foolish; When the mind is harmonized, all fetters are released."
"With a mind settled in tranquility and free from delusion, one crosses the ocean of birth and death.
Thereupon, after the deva had spoken this verse, the Buddha remained silent, signifying his approval.
Seeing that the Buddha was silent, the devas knew he had accepted their words; they then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and suddenly vanished.
At dawn, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"In the past, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there were two groups of merchants, each consisting of five hundred men, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Each had gathered their capital and provisions, intending to outfit ships to cross the ocean."
Having finished the preparations, he unfastened the moorings, hoisted the sails, and set out.
Riding the wind straight ahead, he soon reached the Isle of Jewels.

The island was abundant and prosperous, possessing many garments, food and drink, bedding, and seating furniture, as well as exquisite women and all manner of miscellaneous treasures; there was nothing that was not present there.
A certain caravan leader said to the multitude:

"For the sake of our wealth, we have toiled with body and soul to cross the sea and arrive here; what we sought has now been obtained. We should now remain here and delight ourselves with the five kinds of sensory pleasures."
The second caravan leader addressed his followers:
"Although this place abounds in various treasures, the five kinds of music, and beautiful women, and lacks nothing in terms of food and clothing, we ought not to dwell here for long."

At that time, there was a goddess in the void who, out of compassion for these merchants, wishing to fulfill their heart’s desires so they might obtain much wealth and return home in safety, spoke to the merchants from mid-air:
"Although there is wealth, the five pleasures, beautiful maidens, clothing, and food and drink here, it is not a place where one should dwell long; you should return home early."
"Why is this? Seven days from now, this entire land shall be submerged by water.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Furthermore, there was a celestial maiden of Māra who intended to cause these merchants to perish right there so that they could not return home; she announced from mid-air, saying:
"Gentlemen, there is no need for you to prepare your carriages to depart. Here is a place of joy, most worthy of entertainment."
Originally there was no water here; even if water were to reach this place, by what means could these various jewels, food and drink, clothing, maidservants, and the five kinds of music exist?
"What was said the day before yesterday—that the water would submerge this place—is all false and not to be trusted.
Having spoken thus, she vanished.
Upon hearing the celestial maiden’s words, the first merchant leader commanded his followers:
"O you, do not further prepare your carriages with the intent to return; do not believe what was previously said by the celestial beings, for that was merely false.

Herein lies happiness, where the five desires are never lacking. It was precisely for the sake of seeking this that you toiled so hard in Jambudvīpa; now that you have already attained it, for what reason would you depart again?"
The second caravan leader returned and addressed his followers:
"Gentlemen, do not be greedy for the five pleasures and remain here for long.
Seven days from now, the waters shall fill this place; quickly go to market, prepare your carriages, and repair your ships."
What I said the day before yesterday was sincere and not false.
Even if there were no water for seven days, I would still have prepared myself to return; how could I possibly abandon my father, mother, wife, and children?
"If after seven days the waters do not arrive, you may then amuse yourselves here with these five pleasures before returning leisurely.
But if the waters truly come as previously described by the gods, once our preparations for departure are complete, what difficulty will there be in leaving?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Seven days from now, just as previously stated by the first caravan leader, the water shall fill that land.
At that time, the second caravan leader, having already made his preparations, will have his entire retinue board the ship on the day the water arrives."

The first merchant leader had not previously prepared his defenses; on the day the waters rose, he vied for a boat with those who were already prepared. The boat owner protected it and would not allow him to advance, so the leader donned armor and took up a staff, engaging in combat with them.
The second merchant, while on the ship, used a spear to pierce the foot of the first merchant; it passed all the way through, and he immediately died.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who the first merchant was?"
Devadatta was that [first] merchant;
the second merchant who struck the first merchant with a spear was I myself;
and those five hundred merchants, the first group of five hundred, were the five hundred disciples of Devadatta at present.
At that time, the second merchant with his five hundred followers were these present five hundred arhats;

At one time the Buddha was at the Great Anavatapta Spring, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats possessing the six supernormal powers and the faculty of spiritual travel, with the single exception of one bhikṣu—Ānanda.

At that time, he was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, together with a great assembly of sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats."
Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata Sarvābhibhū had two kinds of bhikṣus:
one kind of bhikṣu was named Anabhibhū, and the other kind of bhikṣu was named Nityapramudita.
The bhikṣu Asaṃjaya possessed the six supernormal powers;
the bhikṣu Nityapramudita had not yet eliminated his fetters and afflictions.
At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was an elder named Mahāpriya, who possessed elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, with inexhaustible wealth and resources.
The householder Mahāpraṇāda had a wife named Sujātā, who was peerlessly beautiful.
Two kinds of bhikṣus frequented her home, serving as her patrons (dānapati).
The skillful illusory wife provided the monk Anābhibhū with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; these four requisites were never lacking.
She constantly delighted in making offerings, though they were quite meager.
Why is this? It is because the monk Wu-sheng has severed all outflows and is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers;
whereas the monk Chang-huan has not yet exhausted his fetters and has not yet attained the Way.
The bhikṣu Changhuan saw that the bhikṣu Wusheng was receiving preferential offerings and gave rise to feelings of jealousy; he slandered him out of malice, saying:
"The bhikṣu Wusheng has a liaison with Shan Huan; he does not provide offerings for the sake of the Dharma, but offers them out of personal affection alone."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you know who that disciple of the Tathāgata Viśeṣagāmin named Nityapramudita was at that time?
It was none other than myself."
"If you wish to know who that skillful illusory woman was, it was this Brahmin girl named Cañcā here.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"At that time, I groundlessly slandered the Arhat Anīya. Because of this sin, for countless thousands of years, I suffered various agonies within the hells."

Now, although I have attained Buddhahood, when I am preaching the Dharma for the sake of the six heretical teachers, the assembly of bhikṣus—both those whose outflows are exhausted and those whose are not—as well as kings, ministers, commoners, and faithful laymen and women, because of the remnants of my past karma, the garrulous girl Mādrī, carrying a basin and with her belly swollen, comes before me and says:
"Why, Śramaṇa, do you not speak of your own household affairs?"
He then spoke of another matter:
"Are you enjoying yourself alone today? Do you not know of my suffering?
For what reason?"
"You previously had an illicit affair with me, which caused me to become pregnant. Now that my time is near, I require ghee and oil to nourish the infant; you must provide all of these for me."
At that time, the entire assembly lowered their heads and remained silent.

Then Śakra-devānām-indra, who was attending the Buddha behind him fanning him, used his supernormal power to transform himself into a mouse. It entered the lining of his robe and gnawed at the cord of his water vessel, causing it to suddenly fall to the ground.

At that time, the fourfold assembly of disciples and the followers of the six heretical teachers, seeing the basin fall to the ground, were all filled with great joy. They raised their voices in celebration and laughed with boundless delight, shouting in unison:
"You dead, blood-stained, sinful wretch! How could you conceive such an evil intent as to slander the pure, unsurpassed, true, and correct [Dharma]?"
"This earth is ignorant indeed, that it can tolerate such an evil being!
As each of the assembly spoke thus, the earth immediately split open, and a mass of flaming fire surged forth; the woman fell into it and went straight to the great Avīci hell.
When the great assembly saw this woman’s body fall into hell, King Ajātaśatru was struck with terror; his hair stood on end, and he immediately rose, joined his palms, knelt on both knees, and said:
“Where is the place where this woman has now fallen?”
The Buddha replied to the Great King,
"The place where this woman has fallen is named Avīci Niraya.
King Ajātaśatru asked the Buddha again:
"This woman did not kill anyone, nor did she steal; she merely spoke a falsehood, and yet she has fallen into Avīci?
The Buddha said to King Ajātaśatru:
"The dependent origination of dharmas that I have taught consists of superior, middling, and inferior levels, as well as the actions of body, speech, and mind."
King Ajātaśatru asked again:
"Which is grave? Which is middling?"
"What is considered inferior?
The Buddha said to King Ajātaśatru:
"Mental action is the most serious; verbal action is intermediate; physical action is inferior."
King Ajātaśatru questioned the Buddha again, and the Buddha replied:
"The manifestation of coarse conduct through the body can be seen;
that which is practiced through speech is what is heard by the ear."
"These two matters are what is heard and seen in the world.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"As for mental activity, when a thought arises, there is no one who hears or sees it; this is an internal matter."
"All conditioned phenomena are bound by the nail of the mind.
The King asked the Buddha again, "The mind cannot be seen; why then is it said that the mind alone is the binding nail?"
The Buddha replied to the king:

"If a man or a woman intends to commit the acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct with their own bodies, they must first reflect: 'At what time during the morning, midday, or evening may I act? To what place may I go?'"
The Buddha spoke again to the king:
"When a person performs an action, they first deliberate with their mind and only then carry it out; therefore, it is bound by the nail of the mind, not by body or speech."
The Buddha spoke again to the king:
"Regarding this practice of speech, when one intends to engage in verbal conduct, one first reflects with intention:
'If I am in a great assembly and discourse upon the Dharma;'"
If, while sitting in the assembly and deliberating upon the Vinaya, someone were to question me, I would contradict their statement, saying: "This matter is not one concerning our own affairs;
if there are such words, I shall oppose them, for they speak thus only because they have received the influence of another's intent."
If, while practicing these three things, one is not yet free from attachment, one should further devise a plan and go to fight them, saying:
"They wish to kill you, break you, and destroy you; you should follow my words and do not trust others."
"If one engages in such divisive speech, one becomes hypocritical and destroys the True Dharma; after the end of life, one will fall into hell.
The Buddha said to the king:
"Therefore, verbal actions are bound by the nail of the mind, not by the body or speech."
The king asked the Buddha again,
"For what reason?
The Buddha replied to the king:

"The three [actions] of the body and the four [actions] of speech are all fastened to the nail of the mind. If the mind does not intend them, the body cannot act alone; therefore, the body and speech are fastened to the nail of the mind."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Having thoroughly contemplated within the mind, One then performs two actions.
One feigns shame regarding body and speech, Yet never feels remorse in the heart and mind."
"First one should feel shame in the mind, and only thereafter feel shame in body and speech;
these two do not exist apart from the mind, nor can they function independently.
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, wept and was moved by deep sorrow.
The Buddha asked the king,
"Why are you weeping? The king replied:
“Because sentient beings lack wisdom and do not understand these three matters, they are constantly subject to decline; for this reason, I feel compassion.
These sentient beings consider only body and speech to be great, not realizing that the mind is profound and subtle.”
“World-Honored One!
Originally I considered the body and speech to be great, while the mind was small;
now, having heard from the Buddha, I know that the mind is great, while the body and speech are small.”
The Buddha asked the king:
"Originally, on what basis did you know that body and speech were great while the mind was small;
why do you now claim that the mind is great while body and speech are small?"
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"When a person kills living beings, everyone sees it;
likewise, if they commit theft or sexual misconduct, these are also seen by others. These three physical actions are witnessed by all under heaven."
Speaking falsehoods, harsh words, double-tongued speech, and insincere talk—these four matters of the mouth are heard by all in the world;

Therefore, sentient beings consider what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear to be great.
Now, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, we know that the mind and intention are what is truly great, while the body and speech are small.
"For this reason, the two matters of body and speech are bound to the nail of the mind.
The Buddha again asked the king:
"How do you know that the nail of the mind is great, such that the two matters of body and speech are bound to the nail of the mind?"
The king said to the Buddha:
"This garrulous woman, wishing to bring about slander and defamation, first thought in her mind:
'I shall bind a basin to my belly and, in the midst of the great assembly, speak of such matters.'"
"Furthermore, having heard what the Buddha has taught, I therefore know that the mind is great, while the body and speech are small.

The King replied,

The Buddha said: “Excellent! Excellent!”
